summary:
Casanare department stands under the national framework of Colombia, where the legal position a trans visitor meets is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015 the sex marker on government-issued identification has been changed by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments, and Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016, adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

Further national provisions define the formal legal exposure of a visitor to the department. Homosexuality was decriminalised in 1981, Congress passed a law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation in 2011, passports issued within Colombia have offered three gender options including X since August 2023, adults may change legal gender before a notary with a free simultaneous name change on first request, and gays, lesbians and bisexuals have served openly in the armed forces since a 1999 court ruling. Casanare has no separate legal regime of its own.

The practical risk is set by enforcement rather than statute. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025; other counts put 41 trans people killed in 2023, eight between February and April 2024, and 13 in the first quarter of 2025. CNN's 'As Equals' feature of 6 August 2025 documented that killings did not stop after the attack on Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, in Bello, Antioquia in April 2025, and reported gangs linked to queer and transgender deaths.

Armed-group "social cleansing" campaigns are the sharpest documented pattern, and they sit in other departments. In Caquetá, flyers on the streets and via WhatsApp named "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets, a trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men she had one week to leave town and fled at night, and a second trans woman said a friend was killed. In Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". Casanare falls under the national kill figures and this armed-group pattern; the sources contain no Casanare-specific finding of local aggravation and none of local protection.
tangentialFactors:
The gap between statute and daily experience is the finding of the UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, who completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms while warning that institutional progress and lived experience are disconnected and that killings are rising.

Economic marginalisation compounds the violence risk. The Guardian's reporting from Caquetá states that discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work, and trans women in that department reported few options beyond sex work; a trans salon owner, Tatiana Cespedes, was forced to relocate twice after death threats from armed men.

Some of the violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence against them as gender persecution, a crime against humanity, and the UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.

Caquetá and Guajira are the documented benchmarks for armed-group targeting of trans people; Casanare is unmeasured against them rather than demonstrably quieter. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025, so the framework a visitor relies on rests on court jurisprudence and notary procedure rather than a settled statute.
localsOnly:
Residents change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, with a free simultaneous name change on first request and no surgical or psychiatric prerequisite, a route available since June 2015 under Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993.

Same-sex marriage has been available since the Constitutional Court's 6-3 ruling of 28 April 2016, with the first wedding in Cali on 24 May 2016, and adoption rights with dual-parent birth registration were granted by a November 2015 ruling; three rulings between February 2007 and April 2008 had already granted same-sex couples property, social-security and pension rights.

Discrimination based on sexual orientation has been banned by statute since Congress passed the law in 2011, gays, lesbians and bisexuals have served openly in the armed forces since a 1999 court ruling, and identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025 alongside the X passport option available since August 2023.

A Colombian court has also ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports any Casanare-specific legal, enforcement, facilities or violence finding; the department entry yielded nothing usable, so the local picture here is assembled entirely from national and other-department evidence.

Whether armed groups operate in Casanare, whether they have issued threats or kill lists there, and whether the department's own authorities record hate-crime or killing data are unresolved and not sourced in this inventory.

The count of trans people killed in any period is reported differently by different sources (41 in 2023, eight between February and April 2024, 13 in the first quarter of 2025, 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025); the discrepancies in scope and method are unresolved here.
